beats.title: Lesson 2 — S7comm Enumeration
beats.say: Welcome back to CybICS. In the first lesson we mapped the network. Now we focus on one industrial protocol and enumerate a Siemens style controller over S seven comm.

beats.head: What is S7comm?
beats.body:
S7comm is the protocol Siemens PLCs speak, normally on TCP/102. Like most industrial protocols it is unauthenticated and freely answers questions about itself.
  • It reveals the module, hardware, firmware version and serial.
  • Attackers use this to match a PLC to known vulnerabilities.
  • Maps to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS T0846 and T0861.
beats.say: S seven comm is the protocol that Siemens P L Cs speak. It normally runs on port one zero two. Like most industrial protocols it is unauthenticated, and it will happily answer questions about itself: the module number, the hardware type, the firmware version, and the serial number. An attacker uses that identity to match the controller to known vulnerabilities. This maps to MITRE ATT and CK for I C S techniques T zero eight four six and T zero eight six one, remote system discovery and point and tag identification.

beats.head: A service on a non-standard port
beats.body: In this lab the interesting S7 service does not sit on the usual port. From the Kali attack machine we probe the S7comm host 172.18.0.6 and find a second service on a non-standard port.
beats.say: In this lab the interesting S seven service does not sit on the usual port. Defenders sometimes move a service to hide it. From the Kali attack machine we probe the S seven comm host and look at both the standard port and a non-standard one.

beats.caption: Probe the S7comm host - a second port, 1102, is open
beats.say: A quick port scan of the S seven comm host shows the standard port one zero two is closed here, but a second port, one one zero two, is open. The name nmap prints next to it is only a guess from a static list, so we cannot trust it. We need to ask the service what it really is.

beats.head: The tool won't look there
beats.body: Nmap ships an s7-info script that fingerprints S7 PLCs — but its trigger, the portrule, is hard-coded to port 102. On a non-standard port it simply never runs.
beats.say: Nmap ships a script called s seven info that fingerprints S seven P L Cs. But the script has a catch: its trigger, called the port rule, is hard coded to port one zero two. On a non-standard port, the script simply never runs.

beats.caption: The s7-info script only fires on port 102
beats.say: We can see that in the script itself. The port rule matches only port one zero two. So against our service on one one zero two, s seven info gives us nothing.

beats.caption: Teach the script about port 1102, then confirm the change
beats.say: So we teach the script about the new port. A single edit adds one one zero two to the port rule. Now s seven info will fire on both ports.

beats.caption: Fingerprint the PLC - the flag is in the Module Type field
beats.say: We run the scan again. This time s seven info queries the controller on one one zero two and returns its full identity: a S seven three hundred module, firmware two point six point nine, and the system name. And in the module type field, the flag: CybICS, s seven comm analysis complete.

beats.head: What we learned
beats.body:
• S7comm leaks a controller's exact model and firmware, unauthenticated.
  • Hiding a service on a non-standard port is not security — a port scan finds it.
  • Tools can be adapted; the s7-info portrule was a one-line change.
beats.say: To recap: S seven comm hands an attacker the exact model and firmware of a controller, with no authentication. Moving the service to a non-standard port did not hide it; a port scan found it, and adapting the tool took a single line. This kind of fingerprinting is the first step of a targeted P L C attack.

beats.caption: Submit the flag in the CybICS dashboard - on the attack machine
beats.say: Now we complete the challenge on the attack machine itself. In the VM's own browser we open the CybICS dashboard, go to the S seven comm enumeration challenge, paste the flag we recovered from the module type field, and submit it. The dashboard marks the challenge solved.

beats.title: Flag captured: CybICS(s7comm_analysis_complete)
